extracted.intended_audience: researchers, inventors, and patent practitioners seeking US patent protection for natural-product-derived compounds and formulations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on evaluating and drafting patent claims for isolated natural products, extracts, derivatives, formulations, methods, and product-by-process claims in the United States in light of Myriad, Mayo, and USPTO examination guidance. Includes strategy and disclosure recommendations to improve patent eligibility and enforceability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligible subject matter exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are excluded from patent-eligible protection; an invention must be new and useful to be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural products discovered rather than invented may fall into these exclusions and be ineligible even if isolated. Patent eligibility (subject matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101) is conceptually distinct from patentability (novelty, non-obviousness, industrial applicability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-of-nature / 'markedly different' standard
rubrics_metrics.description: An isolated natural product is patent-eligible only if it is 'significantly' or 'markedly' different from what exists in nature; mere isolation/purification is insufficient unless it yields differences 'in kind' rather than 'in degree'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts give inconsistent rulings, but examples: recrystallized aspirin and purified adrenalin were patentable because they were therapeutically different; purified tungsten and naturally-occurring bacterial strains were not because they retained natural properties. The USPTO guidance directs weighing factors for or against eligibility and emphasizes that 'a marked difference must be a significant difference, i.e., more than an incidental or trivial difference.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural difference as primary criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Structural differences between the claimed product and the natural counterpart are a primary (though not exclusive) factor favoring patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Words like 'isolated', 'recombinant', and 'synthetic' add no weight by themselves. A non-naturally-occurring structural derivative (e.g., a methylated derivative) is likely patent-eligible under USPTO examples; an isolated gene whose sequence is identical to a natural gene is not, because the structural difference was not deemed 'marked.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional differences may support eligibility but are not mandatory
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a structural difference, a claimed natural product must exhibit new functions or characteristics that rise to the level of 'marked' differences to be eligible; functional differences are considered but are not necessarily decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A product whose purification results in therapeutically different properties may be patentable; however, courts have also held that functional or commercial usefulness attributable to intrinsic natural qualities does not establish patentability. The USPTO guidance treats functional differences as secondary to structural differences for chemical products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myriad-specific rule for genetic material
rubrics_metrics.description: Isolated DNA with an identical sequence to a natural gene is patent-ineligible; complementary DNA (cDNA) that removes introns may be patent-eligible, but short cDNA indistinguishable from natural DNA may not be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court in Myriad held that mere severing/isolation of genetic material that leaves the genetic information unchanged does not create patentable subject matter; claims expressed primarily in terms of genetic information will be scrutinized for whether the patentee 'created' anything new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility of synthetic derivatives and non-naturally-occurring compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Synthetic derivatives of natural products that are non-naturally-occurring and structurally different are likely patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO examples (e.g., 5-methyl amazonic acid) show that synthetic derivatives with marked structural differences are treated as patentable subject matter. Total synthesis of a natural product may still raise issues depending on whether the compound itself is distinguishable from the natural counterpart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition claims for combinations of natural products
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition made from multiple natural products remains a product of nature if the combination shows no 'marked' difference; compositions are patent-eligible only if the combination results in significantly different properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a composition that achieves synergistically enhanced efficacy at lower dosage (sustained-release hydrogel + paclitaxel) may satisfy the 'marked difference' requirement. If no marked difference, composition claims will be treated as not patent-eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-use claims must be practical, specific, and non-preemptive
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that use natural products must recite practical, specific, and significant applications so as not to merely recite natural principles or foreclose others from using the same natural product in other ways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should avoid: (i) general instructions to use the product; (ii) well-understood, purely conventional, or routine steps; or (iii) steps that everyone must use to apply the product. Good practice: include specific regimens, dosages, routes, and treatment schedules (e.g., administering amazonic acid 0.76–1.25 teaspoons daily for 10–20 days) to limit scope and survive eligibility scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of manufacturing and preparation methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods of preparing natural products (extraction, synthesis, formulation) can be patentable subject matter if they meet statutory requirements like novelty and non-obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the product itself may be ineligible, novel and non-obvious process claims (method of extracting paclitaxel, method of synthesizing paclitaxel) are generally permissible. Process claims should be drafted and prosecuted separately from product claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claim limitations and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are allowed when a product cannot be adequately defined by composition or structure, but in the U.S. patentability is determined by the product itself, not by the process used to make it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed product is identical or obvious over a known product, a product-by-process claim will be unpatentable even if produced by a novel process. The process is relevant only when it 'imparts distinctive structural characteristics' to the product or the structure is otherwise implied by process steps. For infringement, courts often consider both product and process; some decisions hold product-by-process claims cover only products made by the recited process, so accused products made by different processes may not infringe. To broaden protection, draft both process claims and product-by-process claims and disclose as many characterizing features as possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for product distinctiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants bear the burden to prove that a product obtained by a process is non-naturally-occurring and markedly different from natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant cannot prove marked differences, product-by-process claims risk invalidation. Researchers are advised to include all features and available information to characterize the products in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient written description and enablement for broad claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting general formulas or broad genus scope must be supported by sufficient disclosure such that a person skilled in the art would recognize the full scope; mere disclosure of a few species may not enable a broad genus claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: listing only CH4 and C3H8 does not support a claim to CnH2n+2 generally. Provide detailed descriptions of embodiments, substitutions, and variations (including parameters like temperature, pH, reagents) to enable and support broader claim scope. Disclose as many foreseeable embodiments as possible to strengthen written description and enablement support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim drafting strategy for natural-product inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus claim drafting on modifications (derivatives), optimized formulations/dosages, new uses/applications, and advanced preparation/manufacturing methods rather than mere isolation of natural products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims with reasonable scope, include specific and significant limitations, identify and characterize individual embodiments and combinations to achieve broader coverage and enforceability. Frequent review of evolving case law and USPTO policy is recommended to adapt strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement and scope considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process and poorly characterized product claims may confer limited protection and be difficult to enforce; scope of claims should be carefully considered relative to how accused products are made and used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because product-by-process claims may not cover products made by different methods and lack explicit characteristics, enforcement can be challenging. To reduce risk, include both product and process claims, and provide as much structural/characterizing data as possible in the specification.
